activities.anchor: the ship is not a lump of steel
activities.caption: drag the divider — the ball bearing and the envelope
activities.name: naEnvelopeCompare

config.prompt: A solid ball sinks; a quarter-million tonnes of the same metal floats. Drag the divider between the two ways of arranging steel:

before.label: Solid ball bearing
before.text: Density nearly eight times that of water, all the way through. Buoyancy is an average-density game, and a solid body's average is the metal itself — it sinks.

after.label: Steel envelope full of air
after.text: Steel, cargo, fuel, crew and all that air, divided over the whole volume. The average is deliberately kept below the density of seawater — the hull sinks only until it displaces exactly its own weight of water.

config.why: A ship is a submarine that has decided to spend its life on the surface: same material, lower average density.

activities.anchor: loading crews think in centimetres of draft
activities.caption: call the load — TPC at work
activities.name: naTpcEstimate

config.prompt: A bulk carrier with a 6,000 m² waterplane (TPC ≈ 60) is loaded 15 cm deeper. Roughly how many tonnes came aboard?
config.why: 15 centimetres at about 60 tonnes per centimetre ≈ 900 tonnes — each centimetre of added draft swallows A × 0.01 × 1.025 tonnes of seawater weight.
config.context: A 6,000 m² waterplane runs about 60 tonnes per centimetre of immersion.

activities.caption: pair each hull with its coefficient
activities.name: naCbMatch

config.prompt: Hull fullness in one number. Pair each item with its partner:

pairs.right: C_B around 0.8 — underwater body nearly fills its bounding box

pairs.left: the bounding box L × B × T
pairs.right: length, beam and draft multiplied together

config.why: No propeller pushes a brick efficiently, and no tanker is wasted on racing — the number says what the hull is for.

activities.caption: rebuild the heel — from wave to couple
activities.name: naHeelOrder

config.prompt: A wave heels a stable ship a few degrees. Rebuild the chain of consequences:
items: Upright and undisturbed: G sits directly above B, and the two forces cancel in a straight line
A wave heels the ship a few degrees
The underwater wedge on the high side emerges; a new wedge submerges on the low side
B slides sideways toward the submerged side, while gravity still pulls straight down through G
Two equal, opposite forces now act along lines that no longer align — a couple is born
config.why: Which way the couple turns decides the ship's fate: heel moves B outward from under G, and the offset between the force lines is the righting arm.

activities.caption: find the faulty line — the inclining experiment
activities.name: naInclineSpot

config.prompt: A cadet's worked inclining experiment contains one faulty line — click it:
lines: Move a known weight a known distance across the deck: w·d = 10 t × 10 m = 100 tonne-metres.
Read the resulting heel angle from plumb lines: 0.25° on a 10,000-tonne ship.
A larger heel for the same weight shift would mean a larger GM — the ship resisted harder.
config.correction: Inverted: GM = w·d ⁄ (Δ·tan θ), so a larger tan θ for the same shift means a smaller GM — the ship gave way more easily.
config.why: The heel angle sits in the denominator: a bigger observed tilt for the same shift is the signature of less initial stability, not more.

activities.anchor: erase the entire designed stability margin
activities.caption: file each move — margin lost or kept
activities.name: naSurfaceBuckets

config.prompt: The free-surface correction scales with tank area, not liquid volume. File each move:
buckets: Helps — cuts the free surface or the rise of G

items.label: a tank left half-full of fuel
the tank's width divided by baffles into three compartments
a shallow pool of water spread across a wide compartment
the same tonnage of water frozen solid in the same space
loose liquid that runs to the low side on every roll

config.why: Divide a tank's width into three and the free-surface moment falls by a factor of nine — which is why ballast sequences and sounding logs are stability documents.

activities.anchor: the danger is not the water's weight
activities.caption: true or false — water in the bilge
activities.name: naBilgeJudge

statements.s: A little water sloshing in the bilge is harmless because it sits at the bottom, below the waterline.
statements.why: It is the water's movement: every roll slides a wide pool toward the low side, dragging G with it.

statements.s: The same tonnage of water frozen solid in the same space would barely matter.
statements.why: A solid cannot run to the low side — no free surface, no moving G.

statements.s: A shallow pool across a wide compartment has a small free surface.
statements.why: It has a huge free surface — the correction scales with area, not volume.

statements.s: Ships with acceptable paper stability have capsized from bilge water alone.
statements.why: A virtual rise of G can wipe out the paper margin without a single gram of cargo leaving the ship.

activities.caption: you are the designer — choose the GM target
activities.name: naGmBranch

config.root: A new coastal ferry is on your drawing board. What GM do you target, and how do you verify it?

choices.label: Maximise GM — the biggest righting lever the hull can carry
choices.feedback: A stiff ship snaps back upright hard and fast: short roll period, punishing lashings and stomachs.

choices.label: Keep GM tiny for the gentlest possible rolls
choices.feedback: A tender ship rolls gently but holds little reserve against listing forces.

choices.label: Aim in between, then check the whole righting-arm curve
choices.feedback: Large passenger ships commonly run GM around a metre for comfort — and the curve, not one number, decides capsize resistance.

stiff.text: Violent, quick rolling: cargo breaks loose, structures are stressed, crews collapse with seasickness. Comfort, not the maximum, sets the target.

tender.text: Gentle, slow rolls — but little reserve: a modest listing force can produce a list the ship cannot correct.

verify.text: Wind, waves and shifted cargo must not push the ship past her curve's maximum: a healthy GM is the first chapter of stability, not the whole book.

config.why: Designers aim between stiff and tender, and real capsize resistance is described by the whole righting-arm curve — GM alone never guarantees survival.
